claims.text: Adjusting the non-equiatomic composition of an HEA enables systematic tuning of its magnetic exchange interactions.
Composition-induced changes in magnetic exchange interactions tune the magnetocaloric behavior of the HEA.
The initial material contains both magnetic and non-magnetic elements in a disordered lattice.
Varying the relative concentrations of key magnetic elements during synthesis modifies the alloy's compositional profile.
Holding thermal and processing conditions constant isolates composition as the source of changes in magnetic properties.
Non-equiatomic element distributions induce local chemical short-range order.
Non-equiatomic element distributions induce lattice distortions.
Changing the relative concentration of magnetic and non-magnetic species alters the density of local magnetic moments.
Changing the relative concentration of magnetic and non-magnetic species alters the spatial distribution of local magnetic moments.
Changes in local magnetic moments modify magnetic exchange interactions.
Modified exchange interactions shift the Curie temperature.
Modified exchange interactions alter the magnetocaloric response.
Systematic composition changes produce measurable shifts in Curie temperature relative to the baseline alloy.
Systematic composition changes alter the isothermal entropy change relative to the baseline alloy.
Systematic composition changes alter the adiabatic temperature change relative to the baseline alloy.
The tuning effect is significant only when phase segregation is avoided.
The tuning effect is significant only when excessive chemical ordering is avoided.
The proposed tuning approach is primarily applicable to low-dimensional HEA systems in which compositional control dominates other structural effects.
The magnitude of magnetic and magnetocaloric shifts depends strongly on the specific elements selected.
The magnitude of magnetic and magnetocaloric shifts may depend strongly on subtle processing parameters.
